latin_text: CAPUT I. Britanni ante acceptam fidem Christianam idololatræ. De apostolis, qui in Britannicis insulis evangelium primi prædicasse dicuntur : Jacobo Zebedæi, Simone Zelota, Simone Petro, et B. Paulo. De Aristobulo item, et Claudia Britanna.

translation_history.english: CHAPTER I. The Britons idolaters before they received the Christian faith. Concerning the apostles who are said to have first preached the gospel in the British Isles: James the son of Zebedee, Simon the Zealot, Simon Peter, and the blessed Paul. Likewise concerning Aristobulus and Claudia the British woman.

Nam et Origenes^f, quem illi authorem citant, plane contrarium indicat, “terram Britanniæ ante adventum Christi in unius dei religionem” minime consensisse: nominatim vero Andrasten sive Andaten, Victoriæ deam, Dio Cassius^g, Apollinem et Dianam alii a Britannis coli consuevisse prodiderunt: et de eorum idolomania gentilis ipsorum Gildas tam clarum perhibet testimonium, ut res in quæstionem vocari non debeat. Hieronymus pronuntiare non dubitaverit. “Ubi^h tunc totius orbis homines, ab India usque ad Britanniam, a rigida septentrionis plaga usque ad fervores Atlantici oceani tam innumerabiles populi, et tantarum gentium multitudines; Quam^i variæ linguis, habitu tam vestis et armis?

translation_history.english: No one need doubt that, in those times of ancient ignorance which preceded the saving advent of Christ, our Britons and Irish underwent the common lot of the other nations — that is, that they were “without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers as regards the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” For, as the impious Porphyry once said, “neither had Britain, a province fertile in tyrants, nor the Scottish peoples and all the barbarous nations round about as far as the ocean, known Moses and the prophets.” Nor are the learned men who maintain that the Britons were always instructed by their Druids in the worship of one God any less mistaken than Postel was when he trifled in attempting to derive the origin of the Irish from the Hebrews. For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, indicates plainly the contrary — that “the land of Britain, before the advent of Christ, by no means agreed in the religion of one God”; and specifically Dio Cassius has recorded that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons; and concerning their idol-madness their own countryman Gildas furnishes so clear a testimony that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: “Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, common to all the nations, by which the whole human race was bound fast before the advent of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the diabolical monstrosities of my country, almost exceeding in number those of Egypt, some of which we still behold, with their features yet misshapen, within or without the deserted walls, rigid after the usual manner with their grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once deadly but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, &c.” So that the blessed Jerome, in his epitaph of Nepotian, did not hesitate to pronounce upon the most wretched condition of those times and the most happy condition of those that followed: “Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the rigid region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — peoples so innumerable, and multitudes of nations so great; how varied in their tongues, how varied in the fashion of their dress and their arms?”

latin_text: Nam quum temporum plenitudo advenisset, “mysterium^k quod a temporibus seculorum tacitum fuit, factum est manifestum, et per Scripturas propheticas ex imperio æterni Dei ad obedientiam fidei omnibus gentibus declaratum.” Indeque iis qui in tenebris et umbra mortis erant positi, lumen illud gentibus patefaciendum aﬀulsit: de quo apud prophetam Deus; “Constitui^l te ut sis lux gentium, ut sis saluti usque ad ﬁnes terræ.” Christo enim apostolis suis imperante, ut^m profecti in mundum universum, prædicarent evangelium omni creaturæ; egressi illi prædicarunt ubique, ita ut nullum locum cœlesti doctrinæ occultum esse sinerent; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου, non insulas, non continentem, non si quam tertiam habitationem hominibus natura concessit:” quemadmodum Gregorius^n Nyssenus loquitur. Atque ita completum est quod per Esaiam olim Deus prædixerat: “Mittam^o ex eis ad gentes in oceano, insulasque remotissimas, quæ non audiverant famam meam, neque viderant gloriam meam, ut indicent gloriam meam in gentibus.” Nam “verbum Dei,” Augustini verba hæc sunt^p, “non in sola continenti terra prædicatum est; sed etiam in insulis, quæ constitutæ sunt in medio mari: et ipsæ plenæ Christianis, plenæ sunt servis Dei. Non enim separat mare eum, qui fecerat mare.

translation_history.english: For when the fullness of time had come, “the mystery which had been kept silent from the times of the ages was made manifest, and through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, was declared to all peoples for the obedience of faith.” And from this that light, destined to be revealed to the peoples, shone upon those who were set in darkness and the shadow of death: concerning which God speaks through the prophet, “I have appointed you to be a light to the peoples, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.” For when Christ commanded his apostles to go out into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature, they went out and preached everywhere, so that they allowed no place to remain hidden from the heavenly doctrine; “μὴ νήσους, μὴ ἤπειρον, μηδ' εἴτινα τρίτην ἀνθρώποις κατοικίαν ἡ φύσις ἐδίδου [neither the islands, nor the mainland, nor any third dwelling-place that nature had granted to humankind],” as Gregory of Nyssa puts it. And thus was fulfilled what God had once foretold through Isaiah: “I will send some of them to the peoples in the ocean, and to the most remote islands, which had not heard my fame nor seen my glory, that they may declare my glory among the peoples.” For “the word of God,” — these are Augustine’s words — “has been preached not on the continental land alone, but also in the islands, which are set in the midst of the sea: and these too are full of Christians, full of the servants of God. latin_text: Et quidem a primo exortu Evangelii suscepisse Britanglaciali frigore rigenti insulæ, et velut longiore terrarum secessu soli visibili non proximæ verus ille non de ﬁrmamento solum^q temporali, sed de summa etiam cœlorum arce tempora cuncta excedente, universo orbi præfulgidum sui coruscum ostendens tempore, ut scimus, summo Tiberii Cæsaris (quo absque ullo impedimento ejus propagabatur religio comminata, senatu nolente, a principe^r morte delatoribus^s militum ejusdem) radios suos primum indulget, id est, sua præcepta Christus. Quæ licet ab incolis tepide suscepta sunt; apud quosdam tamen integre, et alios minus, usque ad persecutionem Diocletiani permansere." Hæc Gildas; ubi quod de tempore summo Tiberii dicit, ex Eusebii chronico exponendum est: in quo ad annum vel ultimum, vel penultimum Tiberii annotatum est, "Pilato de Christianorum dogmate ad Tiberium referente, Tiberius retulit ad senatum, ut inter cætera sacra reciperetur. Verum quum ex consulto patrum, Christianos eliminari urbe placuisset; Tiberius per edictum accusatoribus Christianorum comminatus est mortem.

translation_history.english: And indeed, that [Britain] received the Gospel from its very first rising — that to this island stiff with glacial cold and, as though lying in some remoter recess of the lands and not near to the visible sun, that true Sun, shining not from the temporal firmament alone but from the highest citadel of the heavens that surpasses all times, displaying to the whole world the radiant gleam of himself, first granted his rays in time, as we know, at the close of Tiberius Caesar's reign (when his religion was being propagated without any hindrance — the senate unwilling, but the emperor threatening death against the informers who denounced its adherents) — that is, Christ granted his precepts. And although these were received tepidly by the inhabitants, yet among some entirely and among others less so, they remained until the persecution of Diocletian.” So Gildas; and what he here says about the close of Tiberius's reign must be explained from Eusebius's chronicle, in which, at either the last or the next-to-last year of Tiberius, it is noted: “When Pilate had reported to Tiberius concerning the doctrine of the Christians, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, that it might be received among the other sacred rites. But when, by the deliberation of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians be expelled from the city, Tiberius by edict threatened death to the accusers of the Christians.

translation_history.english: Some report — from the book on the sufferings of the martyrs by Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic — that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went away into the west and performed many miracles in those regions. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and following him, Freculf of Lisieux. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that he "preached on the western shores before all the other apostles." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who has put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former says, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "On his return James visited Gaul, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest importance." The latter, in his "Speculum Historiale" (and cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, ambassador of the king of Castile), writes thus: "While the apostles were going to the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, having landed on the shores of Ireland, fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephon, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius, that by their fellowship he might root out the tares and commit the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. Jacobi apostoli, et translatione corporis ejus (si tamen idem utriusque operis author non fuerit) non in Hibernia, sed in Galæcia ista facta referunt. “ Novem discipulos in Galæcia,” ait in præfatione sua Calixtus^h, “ dum adhuc viveret, apostolus elegisse dicitur: quorum septem, aliis duobus in Galæcia prædicandi causa remanentibus, cum eo Hierosolymis perrexerunt, ejusque corpus post passionem per mare ad Galæciam deportaverunt. De quibus beatus Hieronymus in suo martyrologio sic dixit, ac beato Chromatio scripsit : quod sepulto in Galæcia beati Jacobi corpore, ab apostolis Petro et Paulo infulis episcopalibus apud Romam ordinantur, et ad prædicandum Dei verbum ad Hispanias, adhuc gentili errore implicatas, diriguntur.

translation_history.english: But others show that James was killed by Herod before the apostles were divided into "the various regions of the world" (as Vincent puts it, following Turpin) — namely, the very authors whom Vincent himself followed. Turpin, in the Life of Charlemagne, and Calixtus II, in the book on the miracles of St. James the apostle and the translation of his body (if indeed one and the same person was not the author of both works), report that these things took place not in Ireland but in Galicia. "The apostle," says Calixtus in his preface, "is said to have chosen nine disciples in Galicia while he was still living: seven of whom, the other two remaining in Galicia to preach, went with him to Jerusalem, and after his passion carried his body by sea to Galicia. Of these the blessed Jerome spoke thus in his martyrology, and wrote to the blessed Chromatius: that, once the body of blessed James had been buried in Galicia, they were ordained at Rome by the apostles Peter and Paul with episcopal mitres, and were sent to preach the word of God to the Spains, still entangled in pagan error."

In vetere Romanæ Ecclesiæ martyrologio, quod suo præfixit Ado, non aliud de illis dicitur, quam quod “ Romæ ab apostolis^o ordinati sunt.” In Britannico vero^p, quod describendum curavit Ricemarchus Sulgeni Menevensis episcopi filius, ne nominantur quidem. In apostolorum tamen catalogo, qui epistolæ ad Chromatium et Heliodorum ibi subjicitur, de Jacobo legitur: “ Hic Hispaniæ, et in occidentalia loca prædicavit: et sub Herode gladio cæsus occubuit.” Addit Ordericus Vitalis Uticensis monachus, libro secundo ecclesiasticæ historiæ, septem ipsius discipulos cadaver ejus in Hispaniam detulisse, “ et a rege Galliciæ susceptos, primum fidem et religionem Hiberis prædicavisse.” An pro Hiberis Vincentius alicubi Hibernis exaratum repererit, aliis conjiciendum relinquo : certe hujusmodi aliquo errore dictos Jacobi discipulos ad Hiberniam translatos esse, a vero non est absimile.

translation_history.english: And so indeed in the Roman Martyrology (which Baronius confirms was once published under Jerome's name, together with a likewise supposititious letter of the same Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus), as also in the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Notker, and Ado, at the Ides of May, we read that “these men were ordained bishops at Rome by the holy apostles, and were sent into Spain to preach the word of God; and when they had evangelized in various cities, and had brought countless multitudes under the faith of Christ,” they at last rested in the said places of Spain. In the old martyrology of the Roman Church, which Ado prefixed to his own, nothing else is said of them than that “they were ordained at Rome by the apostles.” But in the British martyrology, which Ricemarchus, son of Sulgenus bishop of Menevia, saw to be transcribed, they are not even named. Yet in the catalogue of the apostles, which is there appended to the letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus, it is recorded of James: “He preached to Spain and to the western regions, and under Herod he fell, slain by the sword.” Orderic Vitalis, the monk of Ouche, adds, in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, that seven of his disciples carried his body into Spain, “and, being received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians.” Whether Vincent somewhere found “Hiberni” (the Irish) written in place of “Hiberi” (the Iberians), I leave for others to conjecture; certainly it is not far from the truth that, through some error of this kind, the said disciples of James were transferred to Ireland.

translation_history.english: Jerome affirms that St. Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, τὸν τὴν οἰκουμένην σταδεύσαντα, καὶ τῷ περὶ πίστεως δρόμῳ τὸν κόσμον μικρὸν ἀποφήναντα [who traversed the inhabited world, and by his race for the faith made the world seem small] (as Basil of Seleucia speaks of him), "ran from ocean to ocean," "imitating his Lord and the sun of righteousness, of whom we read: His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to the highest part of it, so that the earth would sooner fail than his zeal for preaching"; and that, after his first defense — which he himself mentions in the later epistle to Timothy — having been released by Nero, he preached the gospel of Christ in the regions of the West as well. The words of the apostle are: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but all forsook me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all the Gentiles might hear." On which passage Theodoret says: "When," he says, "having made his appeal, he was sent from Festus to Rome, his defense was heard and he was acquitted, and he set out for Spain, and, running out to other peoples, brought them the light of doctrine"; and, as the same author adds elsewhere, "He brought benefit to the islands that lie in the sea." Whence Venantius Fortunatus says of him: He crossed the Ocean, even where the island makes a harbor, and the lands the Briton holds, and those of farthest Thule.

Fuit autem Aristobulus cognomento Zebedæus, frater Barnabæ apostoli Domini." translation_history.english: Similarly, in Dorotheus's Synopsis as well, we read that Aristobulus was made bishop of Britain; and in the fragment which is published under the name of Heleca, bishop of Saragossa: "Among the Britons the memory of many martyrs is celebrated, especially of St. Aristobulus, one of the seventy-two disciples, who was also called Zebedee (father of James, and of John the martyr, of Mary Salome), who went to Rome with Peter. Then, leaving his household behind, sent into England as bishop, he died a martyr in the second year of the most savage emperor Nero." For so it stands on page 108 of the Saragossa edition. But what I enclosed in the parenthesis must be corrected thus: "Father of James and John, husband of Mary Salome." For on the following page Concordia, the wife of the apostle Peter, is reported to have been the daughter of Aristobulus and Salome. "St. Peter," says the author, "is held in honour in Spain, and his wife Concordia suffered at Rome under Nero, not long before he himself suffered. She was, as M. Maximus teaches in his commentaries on the epistle of St. Peter, the daughter of Aristobulus, or Zebedee, and of Salome; and the mother-in-law also of Andrew, who married another sister of Concordia and of James and John. Now Aristobulus, surnamed Zebedee, was the brother of Barnabas, the apostle of the Lord." Thus he writes; and with him, concerning Peter's taking to wife the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of the apostle Barnabas, the Greeks too agree — in Metaphrastes, in his commentary on Peter and Paul, and in the Menaia, under the day of June 29.

translation_history.english: Here the most ingenious critic conjectures that the word "Scotici" should be substituted for "Scythici" — forgetting that in Claudian, Apollinaris Sidonius, and those ancient writers the first syllable of the name "Scoti" is always read long, and that in old manuscripts "Scotti" was regularly written throughout with a doubled letter. And he is quite in character when he adds that Persons "proves, in his "Conversion of England," that Claudia could not have been an Englishwoman" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness and search for England in Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not trying to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the emperor Trajan, and was consequently set up, without any foundation, as either a Scotswoman or an Englishwoman. And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from chronological reckoning, carries little weight. For even if, in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited, there occur certain poems composed under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, it must be supposed that he died an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer on the Second Punic War — during whose consulship Nero perished, as both other authorities confirm and Martial himself indicates in those verses about Silius: "After he had governed the mighty year with its twice-six fasces — he who was hallowed when the world had been set free — he gave his retirement years to the Muses and to Phoebus, and now frequents Helicon in place of his own forum."

translation_history.english: Obeying the divine precepts without slackness, they completed, according to what had been shown to them, a certain chapel, finishing its walls below round about with twisted wattles, in the thirty-first year after the Passion of the Lord and the fifteenth after the Assumption of the glorious Virgin — unsightly indeed in form, but adorned in manifold ways with the power of God. Respondit, Normannum, e Britanniæ monasterio quod Glastingeia dicitur, monachum. Papæ, inquit, an adhuc stat illa perpetuæ virginis et misericordiæ matris vetusta ecclesia? Stat, inquit. Tum ille lepido attactu caput G. Glastoniensis demulcens, diu silentio suspensum tenuit, ac sic demum ora resolvit; hæc gloriosissimi martyris Dionysii ecclesia, et illa de qua te asseris, eandem privilegii dignitatem habent: ista in Gallia, illa in Britannia uno eodem tempore exortæ, a summo et magno pontifice consecratæ. Uno tamen gradu illa supereminet: Roma etenim secunda vocatur.”

translation_history.english: Malmesbury adds, moreover, in order to confirm the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury, this further testimony: “A certain monk of Glastonbury, Godfrey by name (from whose letter I have taken this chapter), in the time of Henry of Blois, abbot of Glastonbury, was staying in the district of Paris at Saint-Denis, when one of the elder monks asked him of what people he was and where his home lay. He answered that he was a Norman, a monk of the monastery in Britain which is called Glastingeia. ‘Marvellous!’ said the elder; ‘does that ancient church of the perpetual Virgin and Mother of mercy still stand?’ ‘It stands,’ he replied. Then the elder, stroking the head of G. of Glastonbury with a playful touch, held him long in suspense in silence, and at last opened his lips thus: ‘This church of the most glorious martyr Denis and that one to which you claim to belong possess the same dignity of privilege: the one in Gaul, the other in Britain, arose at one and the same time and were consecrated by the supreme and great pontiff. Yet in one degree the latter stands higher: for it is called a second Rome.’”

latin_text: Refert Cæsar Baronius ex^b actis Mariæ Magdalenæ et sociorum, dispersione facta post mortem Stephani, “Lazarum, Mariam Magdalenam, Martham, et Marcellam pedissequam, in quos Judæi majori odio exardescebant, non tantum Hierosolymis pulsos esse, sed una cum Maximino discipulo, navi absque remigio impositos, in certum periculum mari fuisse creditos: quos divina providentia Massiliam tradunt appulisse.” Additque ex historia Anglorum, quæ manuscripta habetur in bibliotheca Vaticana, sed (quod ille tacet, et nos suo loco patefaciemus) nostris temporibus scripta, “comitem ejusdem discriminis Josephum ab Arimathæa nobilem decurionem; quem tradunt ex Gallia in Britanniam navigasse, illicque post prædicatum evangelium diem clausisse extremum.” In PseudoDextri quoque chronico, ad annum Christi XLVIII. similiter legimus; “ Hierosolymitani Judæi vehementer infensi B. Lazaro, Magdalenæ, Marthæ, Marcellæ, Maximino, Josepho ab Arimathia nobili decurioni, et aliis plurimis ; navi sine remigio velisque, ac sine gubernatore eos imponunt, et exulare mandant : qui per vastum mare divinitus delati, ad Massiliensem portum incolumes appellunt.” Et in fragmento Helecæ attributo; “Fama est, Magdalenam Lazari sororem, cum Lazaro, Maximo atque Chelidonio, Marcella, Josepho ab Arimathia, venisse in Galliam Aquitanicam; ibique prædicasse Domini Jesu sanctum evangelium: ut docent luculenter Gallorum historiæ, et est traditio ubique satis recepta illius regionis.” Quod autem de Philippi in Galliis apostolatu habet Freculphus a Malmesburiensi citatus; ex Isidori libro de patribus utriusque Testamenti^c ad verbum expressit. Apud utrumque enim legimus, Philippum Gallis prædicasse Christum, “ barbarasque gentes, vicinasque tenebris, et tumenti oceano conjunctas, ad scientiæ lucem, fideique portum deduxisse.” Neque hic mihi Baronii^d conjectura placet, Isidori ista a Gallis nostris ad Galatas Asiaticos traducentis : multoque minus, nuperi operum Isidori editoris, Jacobi Breulii temeritas, Galatis pro Gallis in ipso textu, sine ulla veteris lectionis commemoratione, reponentis.

translation_history.english: Caesar Baronius relates, from^b the acts of Mary Magdalene and her companions, that when the dispersion took place after the death of Stephen, “Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, Martha, and Marcella her attendant, against whom the Jews burned with the greater hatred, were not only driven out of Jerusalem but, together with the disciple Maximinus, were set on a ship without oars and committed to the sea to certain peril; and these, they relate, by divine providence landed at Marseilles.” And he adds, from a history of the English which is held in manuscript in the Vatican library, but which (a point he passes over in silence, and which I shall make plain in its proper place) was written in our own times, that “Joseph of Arimathea, the noble decurion, was a companion in the same peril; and they relate that he sailed from Gaul into Britain, and there, after preaching the gospel, ended his last day.” In the chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter likewise, at the year of Christ 48, I read to the same effect: “The Jews of Jerusalem, violently hostile to blessed Lazarus, Magdalene, Martha, Marcella, Maximinus, Joseph of Arimathea the noble decurion, and very many others, set them on a ship without oars or sails and without a pilot, and order them into exile; and these, borne by divine power across the vast sea, put in unharmed at the port of Marseilles.” And in the fragment attributed to Heleca: “The report is that Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, came with Lazarus, Maximus and Chelidonius, Marcella, and Joseph of Arimathea into Aquitanian Gaul, and there preached the holy gospel of the Lord Jesus: as the histories of the Gauls plainly teach, and it is a tradition quite generally received throughout that region.” But what Freculphus, cited by Malmesbury, has concerning Philip's apostolate in the Gauls, he copied word for word from Isidore's book “On the Fathers of Both Testaments”^c; for in both I read that Philip preached Christ to the Gauls, and “brought the barbarous peoples, neighbors to darkness and bordering upon the swelling ocean, to the light of knowledge and the harbor of faith.” Nor here am I persuaded by the conjecture of Baronius^d, who transfers these words of Isidore from our Gauls to the Asiatic Galatians; and much less by the rashness of Jacques du Breul, the recent editor of Isidore's works, who substituted ‘Galatians’ for ‘Gauls’ in the text itself, without any mention of the older reading.

latin_text: Nam præterquam quod Isidorus in hoc ipso opere, capite secundo et octogesimo et in officio Toletano, quod^e Gothicum et Mozarabum vulgo appellatur : itemque Julianus Toletanus archiepiscopus in Nahum^f prophetam scribens, et Beda (vel quicunque author fuit collectaneorum et florum ad calcem tertii tomi operum ipsius adjectorum) Philippo Galliam assignant: idemque “ Gallis prædicavisse Christum” legitur, in libello de festis apostolorum, qui in Hieronymiano martyrologio manuscripto habetur, ex quo pleraque omnia in librum suum de patribus novi Testamenti transcripsit Isidorus: illa barbararum gentium oceano conjunctarum mentio, Europæos Gallos, non GalloGræcos ab Isidoro intellectos esse satis evincit.

translation_history.english: For besides the fact that Isidore, in this very work, at chapter 82, and in the Toledan office, which^e is commonly called the Gothic and Mozarabic — and likewise Julian, archbishop of Toledo, writing on the prophet Nahum,^f and Bede (or whoever was the author of the collections and excerpts appended at the end of the third volume of his works) — assign Gaul to Philip, and the same man is read to have “preached Christ to the Gauls” in the little book on the feasts of the apostles which is contained in the manuscript Hieronymian martyrology, from which Isidore transcribed nearly everything into his book “On the Fathers of the New Testament,” that mention of barbarian peoples adjoining the ocean sufficiently proves that Isidore understood the European Gauls, not the Gallo-Greeks.

latin_text: Quod vero Josephi Arimathæensis opera in gentibus Britannicis ad fidem perducendis Philippus usus fuerit, id totum ex Glastoniensium monachorum lacunis haustum est: a quibus et barbari illi manarunt versiculi, ex chronicis quibusdam de rege Arvirago agentibus citati^g: Intrat Avalloniam duodena caterva virorum; Flos Arimathææ Joseph est primus eorum.

translation_history.english: But that Philip made use of the services of Joseph of Arimathea in bringing the British peoples to the faith is drawn entirely from the muddy pools of the Glastonbury monks, from whom also flowed those barbarous little verses, cited from certain chronicles treating of King Arviragus^g: 'A twelvefold band of men enters Avalonia; Joseph, the flower of Arimathea, is the first of them.'

latin_text: Josephes ex Joseph genitus patrem comitatur; His aliisque decem jus Glastoniæ propriatur.

translation_history.english: 'Josephes, begotten of Joseph, accompanies his father; to these and ten others the right of Glastonbury is appropriated.'

latin_text: Atque ex^h aliis, paris elegantiæ, isti: Joseph cum sociis jussit transire Philippus Ad terram Britonum divinum promere verbum.

translation_history.english: And from^h others, of equal elegance, these: 'Philip ordered Joseph with his companions to cross over to the land of the Britons, to bring forth the divine word.'

latin_text: Fert^i hos camisia qui promissum tenuerunt: Navigio ceteri terræ mox applicuerunt.

translation_history.english: 'A shirt carries^i those who kept their promise: the rest soon made land by ship.'

latin_text: Regi consuluit Joseph tunc credere Christum: Arviragus renuit rex hoc, nec credit in ipsum.

translation_history.english: 'Joseph then counseled the king to believe in Christ: King Arviragus refused this, and did not believe in him.'

latin_text: Glastoniæ bis sex hidas dedit Arviragus rex: Joseph cum sociis jura reliquit eis.

translation_history.english: 'King Arviragus gave twice six hides of Glastonbury to Joseph and his companions, and left the rights to them.'

latin_text: Anno trigeno primo post vulnera Christi, Ecclesiam virgis faciunt cum laudibus isti.

translation_history.english: 'In the thirty-first year after the wounds of Christ, these men, with praises, build a church of wattles.'

latin_text: Habetur et hodie Welliæ in ædibus D. Thomæ Hugonis equitis aurati, tabula ænea, columnæ Glastoniensis ecclesiæ olim affixa: cui incisum legitur: “ Anno post passionem Domini XXXI. duodecim sancti, ex quibus Joseph ab Arimathia primus erat, huc venerunt, qui Ecclesiam hujus regni primam in hoc loco construxerunt, quam Christus in honorem suæ matris et locum pro eorum sepultura præsentialiter dedicavit.” Est etiam penes nobilissimum virum, D. Guilielmum Howardum, Thomæ Norfolciæ Ducis filium, ingens tabula, Glastonienses antiquitates undique conquisitas complectens : in qua, inter alia fabulosissima, et ista legimus : “ Joseph ab Arimathia beati Philippi apostoli discipulatui se contulit, atque ejus salubri doctrina aﬄuenter refertus et ab ipso cum filio suo Josepho baptizatus est. Postea vero a beato Johanne apostolo ipsi prædicationi Ephesiorum insudante, beatæ perpetuæque virginis Mariæ paranymphus delegatus est : ejusdem quoque gloriosæ virginis venerandæ assumptioni cum beato Philippo cæterisque discipulis interfuit, atque ea quæ de Domino Jesu Christo atque ejus gloriosa genitrice Maria audierat et viderat instanter per diversas regiones prædicans, ac multos convertens et baptizans ; tandem decimo quinto post eandem gloriosam assumptionem anno, cum memorato filio suo Josepho ad sanctum Philippum in Gallias venit. Ac deinde secundum quod legitur in libro qui dicitur Graal, Joseph ab Arimathia, qui dominum sepelivit, baptizatus a beato Philippo apostolo venit in majorem Britanniam, sibi et semini ejus promissam, cum uxore, et filio Josephe nomine, quem ipse Salvator noster in civitate Saraz prius in episcopum consecraverat.”

translation_history.english: There is preserved even today at Wells, in the house of Sir Thomas Hughes, knight, a bronze tablet, once affixed to a column of the church of Glastonbury, on which the following inscription is read: 'In the thirty-first year after the passion of the Lord, twelve saints, of whom Joseph of Arimathea was the first, came to this place, and they built the first Church of this kingdom on this spot, which Christ in his own presence dedicated in honor of his mother and as a place for their burial.' There is also in the possession of that most noble man, Lord William Howard, son of Thomas, Duke of Norfolk, an immense tablet comprising Glastonbury antiquities gathered from every quarter, in which, among other utterly fabulous matter, I read this as well: 'Joseph of Arimathea devoted himself to the discipleship of the blessed apostle Philip, and, abundantly filled with his wholesome doctrine, was baptized by him together with his son Josephes. Afterwards, while the blessed apostle John was laboring at the preaching to the Ephesians, he was appointed paranymph of the blessed and perpetual virgin Mary; he was also present, with the blessed Philip and the other disciples, at the venerable assumption of the same glorious virgin, and, earnestly preaching through diverse regions the things he had heard and seen concerning the Lord Jesus Christ and his glorious mother Mary, and converting and baptizing many, at length, in the fifteenth year after that same glorious assumption, he came with his aforementioned son Josephes to Saint Philip in Gaul. And then, according to what is read in the book called the Graal, Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord, having been baptized by the blessed apostle Philip, came into Greater Britain, promised to him and his seed, with his wife and a son named Josephes, whom our Savior himself had earlier consecrated bishop in the city of Saraz.'

latin_text: Joh. Capgrav. in vita Josephi. Tabula magna Glastoniensis.

translation_history.english: ^g John Capgrave, in the "Life of Joseph". The great tablet of Glastonbury.

translation_history.english: ^i This most absurd little fable is found on the great tablet of the church of Glastonbury, and in Capgrave, in the "Life of Joseph".

latin_text: Sequuntur deinde portenta illa, quæ in vita Josephi refert Capgravius ex eodem nugacissimo libro, qui sanctum Graal appellatur, cujus auctor Guilielmo Malmesburiensi paulo videtur fuisse posterior ; licet ab Helinando Cluniacensi, Frigidi montis in Gallia monacho, ad annum salutis DCCXX. referatur. Sic enim ille in chronico, a Vincentio^k Bellovacensi citato : “ Hoc,” inquit, “ tempore in Britannia cuidam eremitæ monstrata est mirabilis quædam visio per angelum, de sancto Joseph decurione nobili, qui corpus Domini deposuit de cruce, et de catino illo vel de paropside, in quo Dominus cœnavit cum discipulis suis, de quo ab eodem eremita descripta est historia, quæ dicitur de Gradali. Gradalis autem vel Gradale Gallice dicitur scutella lata, et aliquantulum profunda, in qua pretiosæ dapes cum suo jure divitibus solent apponi, gradatim unus morsellus post alium in diversis ordinibus; et dicitur vulgari nomine Graal, quia grata et acceptabilis est, in ea comedenti, tum propter continens, quia forte argentea est, vel de alia pretiosa materia; tum propter contentum, id est, ordinem multiplicem dapum pretiosarum. Hanc hiſtoriam Latine scriptam inveniri non potui: sed tantum Gallice scripta habetur a quibusdam proceribus, nec facile (ut aiunt) inveniri potest.”

translation_history.english: There follow next those prodigies which Capgrave relates in the "Life of Joseph" out of that same utterly trifling book which is called the "Holy Grail," whose author appears to have been a little later than William of Malmesbury, although it is assigned by Helinand the Cluniac, a monk of Froidmont in France, to the year of salvation 720. For so he writes in his chronicle, as cited by Vincent^k of Beauvais: "At this time," he says, "a certain marvellous vision was shown by an angel to a hermit in Britain, concerning Saint Joseph, the noble decurion who took the Lord's body down from the cross, and concerning that bowl or dish in which the Lord supped with his disciples; and a history of this was written down by the same hermit, which is called the history of the Gradal. Now 'Gradalis' or 'Gradale' in French means a wide and somewhat deep dish, in which costly delicacies with their sauce are customarily set before the rich by degrees (gradatim), one morsel after another, in successive courses; and it is called by the common name 'Graal' because it is pleasing (grata) and acceptable to the one who eats from it, both on account of the container, since it is perhaps of silver or of some other precious material, and on account of the contents, that is, the manifold succession of costly delicacies. This history I have not been able to find written in Latin; it exists, written only in French, in the possession of certain noblemen, and (as they say) it cannot easily be obtained."

latin_text: Vincent. Specul. Historial. lib. 23. cap. 147.

translation_history.english: ^k Vincent of Beauvais, "Speculum Historiale," book 23, chapter 147.

latin_text: Multa vero inde in fabulosa regis Arthuri acta, lingua Anglicana a se edita, transtulit Thomas Malorius: qui Sangreal vocem hic usurpat, ad sanguinis realis notionem proxime accedentem; partem^l enim pretiosissimi sanguinis Servatoris nostri repoſitum hic fuisse fingit: sive in cruce eﬀusi, sive ex suprema Chriſti cœna reservati: de qua Stephanus Forcatulus: “ Britanni^m sacræ illius cœnæ pignus ac testimonium secum attulisse Josephum commemorant: nempe catinum sanctissimis convivis appositum, diutissime in magna ceremonia, tanquam pignus quoddam securitatis Britannicæ; non aliter atque Trojanum Palladium.” Hæc ille: de aucta etiam a Josepho vetere magia Britannica eﬀatum non minus a ratione quam a religione remotum postea adjiciens: “ Auxit^n prodigiosos ritus Josephus Arimathæus, advena Britanniæ plauſsbilis; qui de Solomonis fonte artem hauserat. Fuit namque hic sapiens rex imbutus divinitus secretiore sapientia: incantationes^o composuit, quibus morbi pellerentur, et dæmones fugarentur, non redituri.”

translation_history.english: But Thomas Malory carried much over from that source into the fabulous deeds of King Arthur which he published in the English tongue: he there employs the word Sangreal, which comes very near the notion of 'real blood' (sanguis realis); for he feigns that a portion^l of the most precious blood of our Saviour was deposited here — whether shed on the cross, or reserved from Christ's Last Supper — concerning which Stephanus Forcatulus writes: "The Britons^m record that Joseph brought with him a pledge and testimony of that sacred supper: namely, the dish that was set before those most holy guests, kept for a very long time with great ceremony, as a kind of pledge of Britain's security, just like the Trojan Palladium." So much from him; he afterwards adds, concerning the ancient British magic as likewise augmented by Joseph, a pronouncement no less removed from reason than from religion: "Joseph of Arimathea, a plausible newcomer to Britain, augmented^n their prodigious rites; he had drawn his art from the fountain of Solomon. For that wise king was divinely imbued with a more secret wisdom: he composed incantations^o by which diseases were driven out and demons put to flight, never to return."

latin_text: De duodecim discipulis a B. Philippo in Britanniam missis, Malmesburiensis quidam monachus in eulogii sui libro secundo hunc in modum meminit: “ Anno Incarnationis Domini LXIII. et assumptionis beatæ virginis Mariæ XV. duodecim discipuli venerunt in Britanniam majorem, missi a beato Philippo apostolo ad verbum Dei ibidem prædicandum: quorum primus fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Jesum Christum sepelivit. Quibus rex Arviragus, licet paganus, ne ulterius laborarent, duodecim hidas terræ eis contulit in insula Avalloniæ, quæ nunc dicitur Glastonia. In quo loco ecclesiam in honore beatæ virginis per admonitionem S. Michaelis archangeli, de virgis torquatis muros facientes, construxerunt."

translation_history.english: Concerning the twelve disciples sent into Britain by the blessed Philip, a certain monk of Malmesbury makes mention in the second book of his "Eulogium" in this manner: "In the year of the Lord's Incarnation 63, and the fifteenth from the assumption of the blessed Virgin Mary, twelve disciples came into Greater Britain, sent by the blessed apostle Philip to preach the word of God there; the first of whom was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Jesus Christ. To them King Arviragus, though a pagan, granted twelve hides of land in the isle of Avalon, which is now called Glastonbury, so that they should labor no further. In that place, at the admonition of St. Michael the archangel, they built a church in honor of the blessed Virgin, making its walls of wattled twigs."

latin_text: In chronico^p quoque Glastoniensi anno MCCLIX. exarato, scriptum legimus: "Anno ab Incarnatione LXIII. discipuli sanctorum Philippi et Jacobi apostolorum venerunt in Britanniam: a quibus primum oratorium in insula Avalloniæ, in honore S. Mariæ fuit constructum, in anno post assumptionem ejusdem quinto decimo." Et in ali0^q, a monacho cœnobii S. Augustini Cantuariensis anno MCCCCVI. conscripto: "Rex Yna fuit primus fundator monasterii Glastoniensis. Monachi tamen ibidem aliam prætendunt fundationem a rege Arvirago (filio Kimbelini regis Britonum, in cujus tempore Christus Jesus de Maria virgine natus fuit) et quod ab Arthuro rege dotatum fuit pluribus possessionibus." Item in libro de prærogativis et dignitatibus ordinem monasticum concernentibus, qui a Thoma Walsinghamio scriptus putatur: "S. Philippus apostolus Jesu Christi misit in Britanniam duodecim prædicatores, quorum primus et præcipuus fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Christum sepelivit. Qui Glasconiam venientes, acceperunt possessionem hidarum duodecim, ab Arvirago nobili rege Britanniæ, adhuc paganicis erroribus involuto. Hi per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem, ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerunt anno post passionem Domini tricesimo primo."

translation_history.english: In the Glastonbury chronicle^p too, written out in the year 1259, I read the following: "In the year 63 from the Incarnation, disciples of the holy apostles Philip and James came into Britain, by whom the first oratory was built on the island of Avalon in honour of St Mary, in the fifteenth year after her assumption." And in another^q, composed in the year 1406 by a monk of the abbey of St Augustine of Canterbury: "King Ine was the first founder of the monastery of Glastonbury. The monks there, however, allege another foundation, by King Arviragus (son of Cymbeline, king of the Britons, in whose time Christ Jesus was born of the virgin Mary), and claim that it was endowed by King Arthur with many possessions." Likewise in the book "On the Prerogatives and Dignities Concerning the Monastic Order", which is thought to have been written by Thomas Walsingham: "St Philip, apostle of Jesus Christ, sent into Britain twelve preachers, of whom the first and chief was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Christ. Coming to Glastonbury, they received possession of twelve hides from Arviragus, a noble king of Britain, still entangled in pagan errors. At the admonition of the archangel Gabriel they built a church in honour of Mary, the holy mother of God, in the thirty-first year after the Lord's passion."

latin_text: Johannes Tinmuthensis, ex Glastoniensis monasterii libris, ita rem narrat: "Ex^r quo apostoli in regiones diversas erant divisi ad prædicandum verbum vitæ, sanctus Philippus apostolus regionem Franciæ cum suis discipulis sortitus est: de quibus misit in Britanniam duodecim (quorum primus erat Joseph ab Arimathia, qui et Dominum sepelivit) anno ab incarnatione Domini sexagesimo tertio, et ab assumptione sanctæ Mariæ quinto decimo : quibus duodecim hidæ ab Arvirago paganicis erroribus decepto concessæ erant. Qui ibidem Deo servientes, per Gabrielis archangeli admonitionem; ecclesiam in honore sanctæ Dei genetricis Mariæ construxerant. Cumque fidem Christi constanter prædicarent, rex barbarus cum gente sua tam nova audiens et inconsueta, omnino prædicationi eorum consentire renuebat, nec paternas traditiones commutare volebat: quia tamen de longe venerant, ad petitionem eorum quandam insulam sylvis paludibusque circumdatam ad inhabitandum concessit. Erat enim portio illa duodecim hidarum, et quandam capellam (ut præmittitur) ex virgis torquatis construxerunt anno post passionem Domini XXXI.” Hæc Johannes^s Tinmuthensis, in sanctilogio Britanniæ, et ejus exscriptor Johannes Capgravius in nova legenda Angliæ, sed prudenter præmisso hoc prologo. “ Quæ inferius digesta sunt, apud Glastoniam ex libris monasterii illius excerpsi: quæ si veritatem sapiant, lectoris arbitrio relinquo.” Et hoc ad extremum subjecto epilogo. “ Ego vero in præscriptis et dubiis, et in sequentibus nonnullis, authoritatem discutiendi et definiendi mihi non præsumo: sed tanquam relator simplex, quæ in diversis libris et locis cum laboribus et difficultate sedulus indagator reperire potui, ardua peritis ventilanda relinquens, sine invidia communico.”

translation_history.english: John of Tynemouth, drawing on the books of the monastery of Glastonbury, relates the matter thus: "After^r the apostles had been dispersed into diverse regions to preach the word of life, the holy apostle Philip was allotted the region of France together with his disciples, from whom he sent twelve into Britain (the first of whom was Joseph of Arimathea, who also buried the Lord), in the sixty-third year from the Lord's incarnation and the fifteenth from the assumption of St Mary; and to these, twelve hides were granted by Arviragus, who was still deceived by pagan errors. Serving God there, at the admonition of the archangel Gabriel they built a church in honour of Mary, the holy mother of God. And when they steadfastly preached the faith of Christ, the barbarian king and his people, hearing things so new and unaccustomed, altogether refused to consent to their preaching, nor was he willing to change his ancestral traditions; yet because they had come from afar, at their petition he granted them a certain island, surrounded by woods and marshes, to dwell in. For that portion amounted to twelve hides, and they built a certain chapel (as stated above) of twisted wattles in the thirty-first year after the Lord's passion." So John^s of Tynemouth in his "Sanctilogium of Britain", and his copyist John Capgrave in the "New Legend of England" — though with this prologue prudently set first: "What is digested below I excerpted at Glastonbury from the books of that monastery; whether these things savour of the truth, I leave to the reader's judgement." And with this epilogue added at the end: "For my part, in the doubtful matters written above, and in some of those that follow, I do not presume to myself the authority of examining and determining; but as a simple reporter I communicate without grudging what I, a diligent investigator, was able with labour and difficulty to find in diverse books and places, leaving the harder questions to be sifted by the learned."

latin_text: Polydorus Vergilius, vir naris emunctioris, sublatis crassioribus illis monachorum fabulamentis, historiam hanc ita proponit. “ Joseph^t ille, qui, teste Matthæo evangelista, ab Arimathæa civitate oriundus, Christi corpus sepeliverat, sive casu, sive consilio, ita volente Deo, cum non parvo comitatu, in Britanniam venit: ubi tam ipse, quam ejus socii, cum de evangelio prædicarent, atque dogma Christi sedulo docerent, multi per hæc ad veram pietatem traducti, salutiferaque fruge imbuti, baptizati sunt. Isti viri certe divino spiritu aﬄati, cum a rege parum terræ ad inhabitandum (proxime Welliam oppidum, circiter millia passuum quatuor) dono accepissent, ibi novæ religionis prima jecerunt fundamenta, ubi hodie est templum magnificum cœnobiumque monasticæ familiæ D. Benedicti ordinis nobile. Loco nomen est Glasconia. Hæc omnino Christianæ pietatis in Britannia extitere primordia; quam deinde Lucius rex, sicut paulo post dicemus, prope extinctam baptismi fonte sublatus mirabiliter accendit, pieque adauxit. Nam Gildas testis est, Britannos jam inde ab initio orti evangelii, Christianam recepisse religionem."

translation_history.english: Polydore Vergil, a man of more discriminating judgement, having set aside those cruder fables of the monks, presents this history as follows: "That Joseph^t who, as the evangelist Matthew attests, was a native of the city of Arimathea and had buried the body of Christ, came to Britain — whether by chance or by design, God so willing — with a considerable company; and there, as both he and his companions preached the gospel and diligently taught the doctrine of Christ, many were by these means brought over to true piety, imbued with the fruit that brings salvation, and baptized. These men, assuredly filled with the divine Spirit, when they had received from the king as a gift a small parcel of land to dwell in (near the town of Wells, at a distance of about four miles), there laid the first foundations of the new religion, where today stands a magnificent church and a noble monastery of the monastic family of the order of St. Benedict. The name of the place is Glastonbury. These were altogether the beginnings of Christian piety in Britain, which — when it was nearly extinguished — King Lucius, as I shall relate a little later, having been raised from the font of baptism, wonderfully rekindled and piously enlarged. For Gildas is witness that the Britons received the Christian religion from the very first rising of the gospel."

Nam, ut annalium scriptores prodiderunt, in Britanniam transmigravit; ibique et cultum Christi docuit, et multa sui monumenta in valle Avilonis, quæ adhuc visuntur, reliquit."

translation_history.english: So far Polydore; and before him Richardus Lepidus Bartholinus. "Nor^x has it escaped me," he says, "that Joseph of Arimathea, after he had been wickedly thrown into prison by the Jews, was so miraculously delivered by Almighty God that he was never afterward seen in Judaea; for, as the writers of annals have recorded, he crossed over into Britain, and there he both taught the worship of Christ and left many memorials of himself in the vale of Avalon, which are still to be seen."

translation_history.english: The same account of Joseph's coming is also given by Thomas Scrope, sometime bishop of Dromore in Ireland, in the seventh chapter of the book which he wrote on the antiquity of the Carmelite order; and by Thomas Harfeldius, in his compendium of the kings of the English, where he says that Fagan and Duvian (or Deruvian), in the days of King Lucius, "found in the isle of Avalon an ancient church built by the disciples of Christ, together with ancient writings telling how, when the holy apostles were dispersed to preach, Saint Philip, coming into France, sent twelve of his disciples into Britain, and set Joseph of Arimathea over them." And there is indeed still extant, under the name of our great Patrick, a letter forged by the monks of Glastonbury (this is the charter of St. Patrick cited above from William of Malmesbury), in which he is introduced discoursing as follows on the origin of the church which the Anglo-Saxons called Ealdcirc, that is, "the old church": "The brothers showed me the writings of Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus, in which it was contained that twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James had built that old church in honour of our aforesaid advocate, the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the instruction of the blessed archangel Gabriel; and further, that the Lord had dedicated that same church from heaven in honour of his mother, and that three pagan kings gave to those twelve, for their sustenance, twelve portions of land." And hence William of Malmesbury: "When the twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James came into Britain in the sixty-third year of the Lord's Incarnation, three kings, though pagans, conferred upon them twelve portions of land; whence the name of the Twelve Hides persists to this day." So he (William of Malmesbury) writes in his book "On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury," where he carefully describes the bounds of these twelve hides, together with the principal places contained within their limits; and mention of the same is likewise made in the survey-book of William I, king of the English, which is called Domesday^y, in these terms: "The church of Glastonbury has in that same vill twelve hides which have never paid geld."

translation_history.english: Now a hide is said to be as great a portion of land as suffices to support one family (whence what Bede in the "Ecclesiastical History" calls a familia, his Saxon translator renders Hẏdelandeꞃ), or as much as can be cultivated in a year by a single plough; as our antiquaries^a observe, both from a charter of Dunstan issued in the year 963, in which he grants a portion of land "of seven ploughs^z, which in English is called seven hides," and from Matthew Paris, Henry of Huntingdon, John of London, Thomas Walsingham, and others. But that those three kings — Arviragus, Marius, and Coillus — were pagans, I find noted in the margin of the book of Malmesbury which is held in manuscript in the library of Trinity College, Cambridge; and John Capgrave also intimates the same, although he is hardly consistent with himself on this point. For in the life of Patrick, following John of Tynemouth and Harding in his chronicle^b, he writes that those twelve hides were granted by Arviragus; but in the life of Joseph, that they were granted by two of his successors, Marius the son of Arviragus, and Coillus the son of Marius. Yet John Harding scarcely admits that these kings were pagans. For he relates that Arviragus was converted to the faith by Joseph of Arimathea^c and washed in saving baptism, and that Marius^d and Coillus were to some degree imbued with the Christian religion, although they did not attain to the perfection that was fitting. In the same way Richard^e White of Basingstoke also says that Arviragus was "well disposed toward the Christian religion," and that Coelus too, his grandson by his son Marius, was "instructed for a time in the Christian religion while he lived, yet not so as to profess it publicly."
