Cum ergo Joseph fuerit incarceratus tanto tempore apud Jerusalem, impossibile est eum fuisse in Anglia, cum sit magna distantia.

translation_history.english: In this case, therefore, this negative can well be proved by contrary writing: for the contrary is contained in the Flowers of the Saints, under the legend of James the Less, where it is also read that Titus, entering Jerusalem, saw a certain very thick wall and ordered it to be broken through; and inside they found an old man, who said that he was Joseph of Arimathea, and that he had been shut up there by the Jews because he had buried Christ, and that up to that time he had been fed with heavenly food. In the Gospel of Nicodemus, however, it is said^t that Christ freed him after his resurrection and led him to Arimathea; but it may be said that, once brought out, since he did not cease from preaching, he was shut up again by those same Jews. So far the passage cited above. Since, then, Joseph was imprisoned for so long a time at Jerusalem, it is impossible that he was in England, the distance being so great.

latin_text: III. Potest dici, quod licet hoc fuisset verum, (quod tamen non fuit) non sequitur ergo quod totum solium illud suscepit fidem. IV. Dicitur, dato illo quod negatur, adhuc tamen Hispani primo susceperunt fidem, quod probatur, quia Jacobus martyrium subiit vivente Petro. Scriptum est enin de Herode, quod occidit Jacobum gladio, et apposuit ut apprehenderet Petrum, Actuum capite duodecimo. Sed constat, quod Petrus passus est sub Nerone.

translation_history.english: III. It may be said that even if this had been true (which nevertheless it was not), it does not therefore follow that that whole land received the faith. IV. It is said that, even granting what is denied, the Spaniards still received the faith first; which is proved because James underwent martyrdom while Peter was yet living, for it is written of Herod that he killed James with the sword and proceeded further to seize Peter (Acts 12), whereas it is agreed that Peter suffered under Nero.

latin_text: Nero autem fuit prope annum Domini LIV. et Titus fuit prope annum Domini LXXX. Jam certum est quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoo fuisset postquam de carcere fuisset liberatus per Titum, et sic post octogesimum annum a nativitate Domini: et Jacobus mortuus est ante Neronem pluribus annis, quasi prope quadragesimum annum a nativitate Domini. Et Hispania suscepit fidem a Jaoobo, vivente eo, vel statim in sepultura ejus; ut supra dixi. Ergo Hispania est in fide antiquior." Hæc ad patres Basileensis concilii Alphonsus Garsias: in quibus quædam sunt levia admodum, nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula.

translation_history.english: Now Nero lived around the year of the Lord 54, and Titus around the year of the Lord 80; it is therefore certain that if Joseph had been in England, this would have been after he was freed from prison by Titus, and thus after the eightieth year from the Lord's nativity, while James died many years before Nero, at about the fortieth year from the Lord's nativity; and Spain received the faith from James either while he was alive or immediately upon his burial, as I said above; therefore Spain is the more ancient in the faith." So Alphonsus Garsias argued before the fathers of the Council of Basel — points among which some are quite trifling, and several downright ridiculous.

latin_text: Ad primam ejus responsionem quod attinet: historias et scripta antiqua Josephi ad Britannos legationem confirmantia, quanta potuimus diligentia superius collegimus, atque in medium produximus. Quibus jam addimus oratorum et legatorum regis Angliæ, in hac ipsa synodo propositam assertionem. "Certum est in Anglia reperiri in libris antiquissimis et archivis, præcipue in archivis abbatiæ notabilis Glastonensis, diocesis Bathoniensis; quod Joseph ab Arimathia cum duodecim sociis, aut ex persecutione Herodiana, vel præsidum Romanorum in Judæa, ad Angliam vectus est. Ibidem, quæ de Christo viderat et audierat prædicavit, et prædicando plures convertit; convertendo, multa et infinita sibi, ab illis quos converterat ad fidem collata, conquæsivit; conquæsita postea templo Christo per eum erecto reliquit: (et hoc, tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem:) quod templum a Joseph erectum, in locum religiosum et abbatialem dignitatem translatum est, et laus Christi per notabile monasterium præservatur ad præsens."

translation_history.english: As regards the first of his responses: the histories and ancient writings confirming Joseph's mission to the Britons I have gathered above with all the diligence I could, and have brought them forward; to these I now add the assertion put forward by the orators and envoys of the king of England in this very synod: "It is certain that it is found in England, in most ancient books and archives — especially in the archives of the notable abbey of Glastonbury, in the diocese of Bath — that Joseph of Arimathea, with twelve companions, driven either by the Herodian persecution or by that of the Roman governors in Judaea, was carried over to England; there he preached what he had seen and heard concerning Christ, and by preaching converted many; by converting them he acquired many and boundless gifts conferred upon him by those whom he had converted to the faith; and what he had acquired he afterwards left to the temple erected by him to Christ (and this at the time when Peter was preaching the faith in Antioch); which temple, erected by Joseph, was converted into a religious foundation and the dignity of an abbey, and the praise of Christ is preserved there through a notable monastery to the present day."

latin_text: Sive gestis Pilati apud Gregor. Turonens. histor. lib. 1. cap. 20.

translation_history.english: ^t Or the "Acts of Pilate," in Gregory of Tours, "History," book 1, chapter 20.

latin_text: Probabilitatem contrariam, quam secundo loco urget, negamus omnino esse probabilem. Neque enim aliquem hodie, si Thomam Dempsterum exceperis^u, tam stulte credulum esse existimamus, cui absurdissimum illud commentum, de Josepho muro incluso, probabile videri possit: et de legendæ aureæ authore Jacobo de Voragine, ex^w cujus areolis fœtidi isti sanctorum flores sunt decerpti, in ipsa Hispania a Ludovico Vive^x et Melchiore Cano^y jamdudum lata est sententia; ferrei oris eum virum fuisse, atque plumbei cordis.

translation_history.english: The contrary probability which he urges in the second place, I deny to be probable at all; for I do not think that anyone today — unless you except Thomas Dempster^u — is so foolishly credulous that that most absurd fiction of Joseph shut up within a wall could seem probable to him; and as for Jacobus de Voragine, the author of the "Golden Legend", from^w whose garden-beds those fetid flowers of the saints were plucked, sentence was passed long ago in Spain itself by Juan Luis Vives^x and Melchior Cano^y: that he was a man of an iron mouth and a leaden heart.

latin_text: Tertium illud, quod totum Britanniæ regnum Josephi ministerio fidem non susceperit; verum quidem est, sed ad rem non pertinet. Nam nec totum regnum Hispaniæ a Jacobo conversum fuisse ipsi Hispani dicent; nec integra regna ab ullo apostolorum Christiana facta esse constat: et de antiquitate, non de universalitate susceptionis fidei instituta est quæstio.

translation_history.english: The third point — that the whole kingdom of Britain did not receive the faith through Joseph's ministry — is indeed true, but it does not bear on the matter; for the Spaniards themselves will not say that the whole kingdom of Spain was converted by James, nor is it established that entire kingdoms were made Christian by any of the apostles: and the question at issue concerns the antiquity, not the universality, of the reception of the faith.

latin_text: Quartum vero et postremum, partim incertis, partim falsis nititur fundamentis. Jacobi prædicationem in Hispania, inter incerta posuit Rodericus Ximenius Toletanus archiepiscopus, in concertatione quam anno MCCXV. in Lateranensi concilio cum præsule Compostellano de primatu habuit. Ejus verba, a Garsia Loaisa e libro MS. bibliothecæ Toletanæ edita, hæc sunt. “ Si^z inducat (Compostellanus) primam divini verbi promulgationem, et plurimorum conversionem ad fidem Christi in Hispania (per Jacobum factam:) qui divinam paginam noverunt, testimonium perhibeant. Ego tantum legi, datam ei fuisse potestatem prædicandi in Hispania: sed interim, cum per Judæam et Samariam divinam legem seminaret, sub Herode Hierosolymis truncato capite exhalavit animam, et Domino reddidit. Quomodo ergo ibi prædicavit, quo nondum ingressus est? aut sine prædicatione, quos, obsecro, convertit ad Dominum?” Nec ex parte altera certum est, quantumvis id ita esse affirmet Alphonsus, “ quod si Joseph fuisset in Anglia, hoc fuisset postquam de carcere liberatus fuisset per Titum, et sic post octuagesimum annum a nativitate Domini.” A Tito enim, anno æræ Christianæ (non octogesimo sed) septuagesimo eversam esse Hierosolymam certum est: quæ vero de Josepho Arimathæensi tunc per eum liberato pro certis assumuntur, nugæ sunt nugerrimæ.

translation_history.english: The fourth and last point rests on foundations partly uncertain and partly false: Rodrigo Jiménez, archbishop of Toledo, placed James's preaching in Spain among things uncertain, in the dispute over primacy which he held with the prelate of Compostela at the Lateran Council in the year 1215, and his words, published by García de Loaisa from a manuscript book in the library of Toledo, are these: "If^z he (the prelate of Compostela) should adduce the first promulgation of the divine word and the conversion of very many people to the faith of Christ in Spain (as accomplished by James), let those who know the divine page bear witness; I have only read that power was given to him to preach in Spain, but meanwhile, while he was sowing the divine law through Judaea and Samaria, he was beheaded at Jerusalem under Herod, breathed out his soul, and rendered it to the Lord — how then did he preach there, where he had not yet set foot? or without preaching, whom, I ask, did he convert to the Lord?" — nor on the other side is it certain, however much Alphonsus affirms it to be so, "that if Joseph was in England, this would have been after he had been freed from prison by Titus, and thus after the eightieth year from the Lord's nativity"; for it is certain that Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus in the seventieth (not the eightieth) year of the Christian era, and the things assumed as certain about Joseph of Arimathea being freed by him at that time are the most trifling of trifles.

latin_text: Apparat. ad histor. Scot. lib. 1. cap. 7. pag. 27. Vid. Melchiorem Inchofer, de veritate epistolæ B. Mariæ ad Messanenses, cap. 13. pag. 71, 72.

translation_history.english: ^u "Apparatus to Scottish History", book 1, chapter 7, page 27. See Melchior Inchofer, "On the Truth of the Epistle of the Blessed Mary to the Messinans", chapter 13, pages 71–72.

latin_text: Jacob. Januens. in legenda S. Jacobi minoris.

translation_history.english: ^w Jacobus Januensis (Jacobus de Voragine), in the legend of St. James the Less.

latin_text: Vives, de causis corrupt. artium, lib. 2.

translation_history.english: ^x Vives, "On the Causes of the Corruption of the Arts", book 2.

latin_text: Can. de locis Theolog. lib. 11. cap. 6.

translation_history.english: ^y Cano, "On Theological Topics", book 11, chapter 6.

latin_text: Guilielmus^a quidem Eysengreineus ex annalibus Anglorum narrat eum “ post urbis Hierosolymæ destructionem apostolis adhæsisse; atque hoc pacto jam senem in Britanniam profectum, in urbe Wellia Christum prædicavisse.” Sed temporis illam circumstantiam in nullis Anglorum annalibus expressam reperit. Glastonienses, et Malmesburiensis monachus in secundo Eulogii sui libro, Josephi adventum ad annum Christi LXIII. referunt: quem ab assumptione beatæ virginis XV. fuisse tradunt.

translation_history.english: William^a Eysengrein, it is true, relates from the annals of the English that he (Joseph) "adhered to the apostles after the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and that in this way, now an old man, he set out for Britain and preached Christ in the city of Wells"; but one finds that circumstance of time expressed in none of the annals of the English. The monks of Glastonbury, and the monk of Malmesbury in the second book of his "Eulogium", assign Joseph's arrival to the year of Christ 63, which they report to have been the fifteenth year from the assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

latin_text: Oratores Angli, ut diximus, in Basileensi hoc concilio, templum a Josepho in Britannia erectum asserunt, “ tempore quo Petrus in Antiochia prædicavit fidem :” et in Constantiensi, “ statim post passionem Christi” eundem Britanniam ingressum esse, et populos ad fidem convertisse defendunt. Quod et cum ipsius Josephi ætate, qui Domino passionem adeunte inter Judæos senator^b honoratus fuerat, et cum iis quæ initio ex Gilda de tempore summo Tiberii Cæsaris produximus, bene quadrat.

translation_history.english: The English orators, as I have said, assert in this Council of Basel that a church was erected by Joseph in Britain "at the time when Peter preached the faith in Antioch"; and at the Council of Constance they maintain that the same man entered Britain "immediately after the passion of Christ" and converted its peoples to the faith — which agrees well both with the age of Joseph himself, who, when the Lord went to his passion, had been an honored senator^b among the Jews, and with what I brought forward at the beginning from Gildas concerning the latter end of the reign of Tiberius Caesar.

latin_text: Collect. Concil. Hispan. a Loaisa edit. pag. 291. et Concil. edit. Colon. an. 1618. tom. 2. part. 2. pag. 317, 318. Vide Baron. annal. tom. 9. an. 816. sec. 49, 50, 51, 52. et bibliothec. Floriacens. Joannis a Bosco, part. 2. pag. 184.

translation_history.english: ^z "Collection of the Spanish Councils", edited by Loaisa, p. 291; and the Cologne edition of the "Councils" (1618), vol. 2, part 2, pp. 317–318. See Baronius, "Annals", vol. 9, year 816, sections 49–52; and the "Bibliotheca Floriacensis" of Jean du Bosc, part 2, p. 184.

latin_text: Eysengrein. cent. 1. part. 6. distinct. 6.

translation_history.english: ^a Eysengrein, century 1, part 6, distinction 6.

latin_text: Johannes enim Hardingius indignus est, cujus hic ulla habeatur ratio : qui^c Josephum per ipsos quadraginta duos a Christi morte annos, non quidem in muro, sed in Caiphæ carcere detentum, sine omni cibo et potu vixisse ; deinde a Vespasiano liberatum, et in Britanniam anno Christi LXXVI. perductum, ibique regi Arvirago et conjugi ipsius Genissæ (quæ Claudii imperatoris filia fuisse fingitur) commendatum fuisse fabulatur. Johannes Balæus, Ossoriensis aliquando apud Hibernos episcopus, eodem illo anno ex vita hac migrasse eum scribit. “ In sancta senectute (inquit^d) Josephus inter discipulos tandem quietam morte carnis dormitionem accepit, in Avalonica solitudine sepultus, anno a Christi incarnatione LXXVI. Mario regnante in Britannia. Postea translatum est ejus corpus ad Glasconiense monachorum collegium, et in pretiosa theca repositum. Neque desunt (inquit ille) qui ex conjecturis habeant, contexuisse illum ad ecclesias Britannorum epistolas quasdam.” Quam conjecturam ut verisimiliorem redderet Guilielmus Eysengreineus, ne a præsente ad præsentes literæ scriptæ putarentur, “ reliquisse insulam et, ut renovaret sui memoriam, scripsisse epistolam ad Britannos” illum fingit: Anglorum hic quoque citatis annalibus ; in quibus tamen neque Britanniam eum reliquisse, neque ejusmodi aliquam epistolam scripsisse, neque alibi quam Glastoniæ mortuum et sepultum fuisse, uspiam traditum invenimus^e.

translation_history.english: For John Harding is unworthy of any consideration here — a man who^c tells the fable that Joseph, detained for the full forty-two years after Christ's death not indeed in a wall but in the prison of Caiaphas, lived without any food or drink; that he was then freed by Vespasian and brought to Britain in the year of Christ 76, and there commended to King Arviragus and to his wife Genissa (who is feigned to have been a daughter of the emperor Claudius). John Bale, at one time bishop of Ossory among the Irish, writes that he departed this life in that same year. "In holy old age," he says,^d "Joseph at last received among the disciples a quiet falling-asleep in the death of the flesh, and was buried in the solitude of Avalon, in the year 76 from the incarnation of Christ, while Marius was reigning in Britain. Afterwards his body was translated to the college of monks at Glastonbury and laid up in a precious reliquary. Nor are there lacking," he says, "those who hold by conjecture that he composed certain epistles to the churches of the Britons." To render this conjecture the more plausible, Wilhelm Eisengrein — lest the letter be thought written by one present to those present — feigns that he "left the island and, to renew the memory of himself, wrote an epistle to the Britons," here too citing the annals of the English; in which, however, I nowhere find it recorded that he left Britain, or that he wrote any epistle of this kind, or that he died and was buried anywhere but at Glastonbury^e.

latin_text: Mar. cap. 15. ver. 43. εὐσχήμων βουλευτής· quod a vulgato interprete, nobilis decurio, redditur, de quo videndus commentarius B. Hieronymi in Matth. cap. 27. et Ludovici de Dieu V. C. in Marc. cap. 15. Et H. Grotii, in Matth. cap. 27. ver. 57. Qui apud Plinium Secundum, lib. 10. epist. 113. Buleutæ in Rescripto Trajani, epist. 114. decuriones appellantur.

translation_history.english: ^b Mark 15:43, εὐσχήμων βουλευτής [an honourable councillor]; which the Vulgate translator renders nobilis decurio [a noble decurion], on which see the commentary of St. Jerome on Matt. 27, that of the distinguished Ludovicus de Dieu on Mark 15, and that of Hugo Grotius on Matt. 27:57. Those who in Pliny the Younger, book 10, epistle 113, are called Buleutae are in Trajan's rescript, epistle 114, called decuriones.

latin_text: Jo. Harding. chronic. cap. 47.

translation_history.english: ^c John Harding, "Chronicle," chapter 47.

latin_text: Bal. script. Britan. Centur. 1. cap. 22.

translation_history.english: ^d Bale, "Writers of Britain," Century 1, chapter 22.

latin_text: Extat vetustus catalogus sanctorum in Anglia sepultorum Saxonice scriptus, ac Latine, a Gotcelino Bertiniano monacho Cantuariensi, Anselmi archiepiscopi diebus editus: et de reliquis in Glastoniensi monasterio repositis libellus alter, Henrici III. Anglorum regis temporibus exaratus. In neutro vero Josephi ulla occurrit mentio.

translation_history.english: There survives an ancient catalogue of the saints buried in England, written in Saxon and in Latin, published by Goscelin of Saint-Bertin, a monk of Canterbury, in the days of Archbishop Anselm; and a second little book, concerning the relics deposited in the monastery of Glastonbury, drawn up in the times of Henry III, king of the English; yet in neither does any mention of Joseph occur.

latin_text: Anno demum MCCCXLV. a Johanne Blomæo Londinensi, cujusdam revelationis sibi factæ prætextu, ab Edvardo III. licentia quærendi corpus Josephi ab Arimathia impetrata est: quam, ex archivis regiis^f in arce Londinensi asservatis a me descriptam, lectori communicare non gravabor.

translation_history.english: At length, in the year 1345, John Blome of London, on the pretext of a certain revelation made to him, obtained from Edward III a licence to search for the body of Joseph of Arimathea; and this licence, which I have copied from the royal archives^f preserved in the Tower of London, I gladly communicate to the reader.

latin_text: “Rex omnibus ad quos, &c. salutem. Supplicavit nobis Johannes Blome de London, ut cum sibi (sicut asserit) divinitus sit injunctum, ut venerandum corpus decurionis nobilis Josephi ab Arimathia, quod infra septa monasterii Glastoniensis in Christo quiescit humatum, et est ad honorem et multorum ædificationem his temporibus revelandum, quærat donec inveniat diligenter. Et quia in quibusdam antiquis scripturis dicitur contineri corpus ejus ibidem fuisse sepultum. Nos, si sit ita, desiderantes monumentum ejus, et venerandas ipsius reliquias, qui redemptori nostro morienti tantum exhibebat pietatis et humanitatis obsequium, corpus ejus de cruce deponendo, et illud in monumento suo novo ponendo, devotis honoribus prævenire; et sperantes nobis et toti regno nostro ex revelatione prædicta gratiam uberiorem provenire: concessimus et licentiam dedimus (quantum in nobis est) eidem Johanni quod ipse infra præcinctum dicti monasterii fodere, et illas prætiosas reliquias juxta injunctionem et revelationem sibi factam quærere valeat in locis ubi melius viderit expedire: dum tamen absque damno dilectorum nobis in Christo, abbatis et conventus dicti monasterii, et ruina ecclesiæ et domorum suarum ibidem id fieri valeat; et quod ad id ipsorum abbatis et conventus licentiam habeat et assensum. In cujus, &c. Teste Rege PER IPSUM REGEM.

translation_history.english: "The King to all to whom, etc., greeting. John Blome of London has petitioned us that — since (as he asserts) it has been divinely enjoined upon him that he diligently search, until he find it, for the venerable body of the noble decurion Joseph of Arimathea, which rests buried in Christ within the precincts of the monastery of Glastonbury and is in these times to be revealed for the honour and edification of many, and because it is said to be recorded in certain ancient writings that his body was buried in that place — we, if it be so, desiring to honour beforehand with devout observances his monument and the venerable relics of him who showed to our dying Redeemer so great a service of piety and humanity in taking his body down from the cross and laying it in his own new tomb, and hoping that from the said revelation more abundant grace may flow to us and to our whole realm, have granted and given licence (so far as in us lies) to the same John, that he may dig within the precinct of the said monastery and search for those precious relics, according to the injunction and revelation made to him, in the places where he shall see it most expedient; provided, however, that this can be done without harm to our beloved in Christ, the abbot and convent of the said monastery, and without ruin to the church and their buildings there; and that he have for this the licence and assent of the abbot and convent themselves. In witness whereof, etc. Witness the King. BY THE KING HIMSELF."

latin_text: Septoniæ enim sepultum fuisse (ea Dorsettensium Sćhaſtesburia est) per errorem scriptum legitur in Jo. Caii historiæ Cantabrig. lib. 1. pag. 23. nam Glasconiæ ibidem, pag. 31. legitur.

translation_history.english: ^e For in John Caius, "History of Cambridge," book 1, page 23, it is found written, by an error, that he was buried at Septonia (that is Shaftesbury in Dorset); for in the same work, at page 31, "at Glastonbury" is the reading.

latin_text: Patent. ann. 19. Edvard. III. part. membran. 8.

translation_history.english: ^f Patent Rolls, 19 Edward III, membrane 8.

latin_text: Apud Westmonaster.

translation_history.english: At Westminster.

latin_text: VIII. die Junii.

translation_history.english: On the eighth day of June.

latin_text: Quem habuerit eventum ista inquisitio, non invenio: ab his tamen qui Glastoniense monasterium viderunt est proditum, et sacellum ibi Josephi nomini dicatum, et tumulum etiam positum fuisse, hoc inscriptum epitaphio.

translation_history.english: What outcome that inquiry had, I do not find; yet it has been reported by those who have seen the monastery of Glastonbury that a chapel dedicated to Joseph's name stood there, and that a tomb also was placed there, inscribed with this epitaph.

latin_text: Ad Britones veni, postquam Christum sepelivi; -----------------------------------------docui, requievi.

translation_history.english: I came to the Britons after I had buried Christ; ----------------------------------------- I taught, I rested.

latin_text: Quibus adde, si libet, et Guilielmi Goodi Jesuitæ narrationem, qui Henrico VIII. regnante Glastoniæ natus et puer educatus est. " Glasconiæ^g extabant (inquit) laminæ æneæ sculptæ ad perpetuandam memoriam, sacella, crypta, cruces, arma, observatio festi S. Josephi ad VI. Calendas Augusti, quamdiu monachi regum chartis munitissime gaudebant: nunc omnia cum ruinis confusa perierunt.

translation_history.english: To these add, if you please, the account of William Good the Jesuit, who was born at Glastonbury in the reign of Henry VIII and brought up there as a boy: "At Glastonbury^g," he says, "there existed engraved bronze plates to perpetuate the memory, chapels, a crypt, crosses, coats of arms, and the observance of the feast of St. Joseph on the sixth day before the Calends of August [27 July], so long as the monks enjoyed the fullest protection of royal charters; now all these, jumbled together with the ruins, have perished.

latin_text: Nemo tamen monachorum unquam scivit certum locum sepulchri hujus sancti, vel designavit. Reconditum abditissime dixerunt, vel ibi, vel in monte, qui monti acuto vicinus, et cui nomen Hamden-hill : et futurum, ut quando reperietur corpus ejus, universus eo mundus confluat præ magnitudine et numero miraculorum quæ fient."

translation_history.english: Yet none of the monks ever knew, or pointed out, the certain place of this saint's burial; they said it had been hidden away most secretly, either there or on a hill lying near the sharp hill (Montacute) and bearing the name Hamden-hill; and that when his body should be found, the whole world would flock there, on account of the greatness and number of the miracles that would be wrought."

latin_text: " Et inter cætera memini me vidisse Glasconiæ in cruce lapidea, quæ sub regina Elizabetha subversa fuit, laminam æneam in qua scribebatur, Josephum ab Arimathæa trigesimo anno post passionem Christi venisse in Britanniam cum undecim vel duodecim sociis, permissumque ei ab Arvirago rege, Glasconiæ quæ tunc erat insula dicta Avalonia, habitare, tanquam solitarios viros et simplices : et quod attulerit secum duo vasa argentea non grandia, in^h quibus erat de sanguine et aqua sacratissima, quæ profluxerat de latere Christi mortui. Crux autem ista erecta est ante multos annos ad denotandam longitudinem sacelli ab eodem sancto Josepho ex vimineis cratibus constructi in honorem beatissimæ virginis; deducta scilicet linea recta a medio illius crucis ad latus sacelli postea lapidibus quadratis exædificati: sub qua item erat olim illud sacellum Sancti Josephi in crypta subterranea. Foris autem in muro hujus sacelli beatæ virginis erant in lapide sculpta vetustissimis literis hæc duo verba, Jesus, Maria. Et confirmant antiqua arma Glasconiensis monasterii, quæ sunt hujusmodi: Scutum album in quo per longum erigitur stipes crucis viridis et nodosæ, et de latere ad latus extenduntur brachia seu rami crucis stipiti consimilia.

translation_history.english: "And among other things I remember that I saw at Glastonbury, on a stone cross which was thrown down under Queen Elizabeth, a bronze plate on which it was written that Joseph of Arimathea came into Britain in the thirtieth year after the passion of Christ with eleven or twelve companions; that he was permitted by King Arviragus to dwell at Glastonbury, which was then an island called Avalonia, as men solitary and simple; and that he brought with him two silver vessels, not large, in^h which was some of the most sacred blood and water that had flowed from the side of the dead Christ. Now that cross was erected many years ago to mark the length of the chapel built by the same St. Joseph of wattled hurdles in honour of the most blessed Virgin — a straight line, that is, being drawn from the middle of that cross to the side of the chapel afterwards built up of squared stones; beneath which, likewise, that chapel of St. Joseph formerly lay in an underground crypt. On the outside, moreover, on the wall of this chapel of the blessed Virgin, these two words were carved in stone in most ancient letters: Jesus, Maria. And the ancient arms of the monastery of Glastonbury confirm this, which are of this kind: a white shield on which the trunk of a green and knotty cross is raised lengthwise, and from side to side extend the arms or branches of the cross, like the trunk.

latin_text: Edvard. Maihew congregat. Anglican. ordinis Benedict. Tabul. 2. pag. 1118, 1119.

translation_history.english: ^g Edward Maihew, of the English Congregation of the Benedictine Order, Table 2, pp. 1118, 1119.

latin_text: Sparguntur guttæ sanguinis per omnem aream scuti.

translation_history.english: Drops of blood are scattered over the whole field of the shield.

latin_text: Utrinque ad latera stipitis, et sub alis crucis, ponitur ampulla inaurata. Et hæc semper denominabantur insignia Sancti Josephi: qui ibi habitasse pie credebatur, et fortasse sepultus esse.”

translation_history.english: On either side of the upright, and beneath the arms of the cross, is placed a gilded cruet; and these were always called the arms of Saint Joseph, who was piously believed to have lived there, and perhaps to have been buried there."

latin_text: Eundem cum sociis ibi fuisse sepultum, in magna Glastoniensium tabula ita traditum invenio. “ Ibi requiescunt XII. discipuli: quorum primas et custos fuit Joseph ab Arimathia, qui Dominum sepelivit. Multi ex paganis per eos ad fidem Christi conversi ac baptizati ibidem requiescunt, quorum, propter eorum multitudinem, non est numerus.” De iisdem eulogii author, libro secundo: “ Ibidem diu commorantes, multisque de dicto regno ad locum confluentibus per eosdem ad Christum conversis, tandem in pace quieverunt. Joseph vero ab Arimathia ibidem sepultus est juxta dictam Ecclesiam [B. Mariæ] cum duabus phialis plenis de sudore Christi sanguineo, quas secum de terra sancta detulerat.” Quis vero inde usque ad Lucii regis tempora loci illius status fuerit, Guilielmus Malmesburienſis his verbis edocet. “Sancti^i igitur memorati in eadem eremo sic degentes, eﬄuentibus multis annorum curriculis carnis ergastulo sunt educti: idemque locus cœpit esse ferarum latibulum, qui prius fuerat habitatio sanctorum.”

translation_history.english: That the same man was buried there with his companions I find recorded in the great table of Glastonbury in these words: "There rest twelve disciples, of whom the chief and guardian was Joseph of Arimathea, who buried the Lord. Many of the pagans, converted to the faith of Christ through them and baptized, rest in the same place; of these, on account of their multitude, there is no number." Concerning the same men the author of the "Eulogium" writes in his second book: "Remaining there a long time, while many from the said kingdom flocked to the place and were converted to Christ through them, they at last rested in peace. Joseph of Arimathea, moreover, was buried in that same place beside the said church [of the Blessed Mary], with two vials filled with the bloody sweat of Christ, which he had brought with him from the Holy Land." What the condition of that place was from that time until the days of King Lucius, William of Malmesbury explains in these words: "The saints^i just mentioned, then, living in this manner in that same hermitage, were, after the passing of many courses of years, released from the prison of the flesh; and the same place that had formerly been the habitation of saints began to be a den of wild beasts."
